etymology: From the ordinary phrase fall off (to decline, decrease; long in English for falling-off of trade or health), sharpened in 2000s hip-hop talk about rappers whose music "fell off" after early success, then applied to athletes, celebrities, and brands. Gen Alpha uses it for YouTubers, games, and trends that are no longer good or popular — "Fortnite fell off," "that YouTuber fell off" — and as a tease for a friend who used to be better at something.
biblical_def: When Gen Alpha kids say someone or something "fell off," they mean it used to be great and isn’t anymore — a YouTuber whose videos got worse, a game nobody plays now. The Christian observation: Scripture knows this pattern well, and it applies it not to games but to hearts. The risen Christ told a church that had once been zealous, "thou hast left thy first love. Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works" (Rev 2:4-5). Paul asked the Galatians, "Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?" (Gal 5:7). Christians can "fall off" — grow cold, drift, lose their first love — and the cure is not shame but remembering, repenting, and returning. And the deepest comfort is that our standing does not depend on our own grip: "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy" (Jud 1:24). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Sometimes games and shows fall off and aren’t fun anymore. But Jesus never falls off — He’s always good. And if we ever forget Him, we can always come right back." To the older child mocking someone who "fell off," he can add: be kind — everyone has seasons.
webster_summary: Slang for decline from former greatness (2000s hip-hop; Gen Alpha for YouTubers and games) — a pattern Scripture applies to the heart that leaves its first love, and answers with remembering, repentance, and the One able to keep from falling.
webster_full: FELL OFF, v. phr. (slang, 2000s–present; Gen Alpha) Declined from former quality or popularity. "That channel fell off after they stopped posting Minecraft."
Decode for parents: mostly about entertainment; occasionally a tease aimed at a friend.
Webster 1828, the root — FALL, v.i. To drop from a higher place; to descend by the power of gravity alone.
scriptures: Rev 2:4
Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Gal 5:7
Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?
Jud 1:24
Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,
corruption_summary: "Fell off" is a harmless verdict on fading entertainment; its sharper use mocks a person’s decline, and its deepest echo is the heart that falls from its first love.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct when a child says a game fell off. The habit to watch is contempt for people in decline — the classmate who used to be good at sports, the aging athlete, the grandparent who is slower now. The culture of constant ranking treats every season of weakness as failure.

Use the phrase to talk about the heart. Ask your child: what would it look like for me to fall off from loving Jesus? Teach Rev 2:5 — remember, repent, return. Then teach Jude 24 — the Lord holds His own. A child who knows both will not fear failure and will not despise the fallen.
roots_summary: Old English feallan → fall off (to decline) → 2000s hip-hop "fell off" → Gen Alpha verdict on YouTubers and games.
usage: "Bro, that show fell off so hard."
Remember from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works (Rev 2:5).
He is able to keep you from falling — Jesus never falls off (Jud 1:24).

etymology: Short for washed up, an early-twentieth-century American expression (theater and sports) for a person whose career or powers are finished — like debris washed up on a beach. Gen-Z and Gen Alpha clipped it to washed: "he’s washed" means past his prime, no longer good, often said of older athletes, older siblings, and fathers trying a trick on the trampoline. It sits beside unc and fell off in the vocabulary of decline.
biblical_def: To Gen Alpha, someone who is washed is past his prime — an old athlete, a grown-up who can’t do the things he used to, a big brother who lost at a video game. "Dad, you’re washed" is a common tease. The Christian observation: this is one of the words where Scripture simply takes the slang and turns it into the gospel. In the Bible, being washed is the best thing that can happen to a person. "Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow" (Psa 51:7). Paul told a church full of former sinners, "such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus" (1Co 6:11). Christ is the One "that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood" (Rev 1:5), and He told Peter, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" (Joh 13:8). As for the slang’s sense — past your prime — Scripture is kind to the aging: the righteous "shall still bring forth fruit in old age" (Psa 92:14). A father can tell a five-year-old: "People say ‘washed’ to mean old and not good anymore. But the Bible says being washed is wonderful — Jesus washes our hearts clean! Has Jesus washed you?" And he can laugh when his son calls him washed, and answer, "Yes — and so can you be."
webster_summary: Clipped washed up (early 20th c.): past one’s prime — a tease at the aging that Scripture turns into the gospel’s best word, "ye are washed."
webster_full: WASHED, a. (slang, from washed up; Gen-Z and Gen Alpha usage, 2010s–present) Past one’s prime; no longer skilled or relevant. "He used to be good at basketball, but now he’s washed."
Decode for parents: affectionate teasing at home; occasionally a sneer at age.
Webster 1828, the root — WASH, v.t. To cleanse by ablution, or by rubbing in water; as, to wash the hands or the body; to wash garments.
scriptures: Psa 51:7
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
Rev 1:5
And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood,
Joh 13:8
Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.
They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing;
corruption_summary: "Washed" mocks the aging and the faded; Scripture honors the fruitful old and makes "washed" the word for every sinner cleansed by Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The slang belongs to a youth culture that measures people by peak performance and treats decline as a joke. In small doses it is family teasing; as a habit it becomes contempt for age, which Scripture forbids: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man" (Lev 19:32).

Redeem it with delight. Few slang words hand a father such an easy gospel line. Let your child call you washed; tell him what washed means in the Bible; ask whether he has been washed by Christ. Then honor the old people in your family loudly, so that he learns age is a crown, not a punchline.
roots_summary: Old English wascan → wash → washed up (early 20th-c. theater and sports) → clipped washed (2010s).
roots_lines: Early 20th c.: washed up, finished (of a career)
2010s: clipped to washed in sports and youth slang
usage: "You can’t do a backflip anymore, Dad. You’re washed." "Washed in the blood, son."
But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified (1Co 6:11).
They shall still bring forth fruit in old age — not washed up (Psa 92:14).

etymology: From flop, imitative of a heavy, loose fall (seventeenth century), which American theater slang of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries turned into a word for a failed show ("the play flopped"). It has meant public failure ever since; Gen Alpha says "flopped" of a video that got no views, a joke nobody laughed at, a test, or a dance attempt, and "flop" or "flop era" of a bad stretch.
biblical_def: Something that flopped failed — a video with no views, a joke nobody laughed at, a cake that sank in the middle. Gen Alpha kids worry a lot about flopping, because their failures can be seen by everyone. The Christian observation: Scripture is full of people who flopped, and it tells their stories on purpose. Moses argued with God; Peter denied Jesus three times; Jonah ran the other way. None of them was the end of the story. "Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand" (Psa 37:24). Paul described a whole life of near-flops: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair... cast down, but not destroyed" (2Co 4:8-9). And after Peter’s worst failure, Jesus came and asked him three times, "lovest thou me?" and gave him a job: "Feed my sheep" (Joh 21:17). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Everybody flops sometimes — even people in the Bible. When you flop, God doesn’t stop loving you. He picks you up, and you try again." A child who learns that early is free to try hard things.
webster_summary: Theater slang for a failed show (late 19th-early 20th c.), now any public failure — answered by Scripture’s stories of flopped saints the LORD upheld and restored.
webster_full: FLOPPED, v. / a. (from flop, theater slang; Gen Alpha usage) Failed, especially publicly. "My video flopped — only six views."
Flop — a failure; flop era — a stretch of failures.
Decode for parents: children fear public failure intensely; this word is a window into that fear.
Webster 1828, the root — FLOP, v.t. To clap or strike the wings.
scriptures: Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand.
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;

He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.
corruption_summary: "Flopped" names failure lightly; the culture behind it makes children terrified of public failure, while Scripture tells the stories of failed saints whom God upheld and restored.
corruption_paragraphs: Children now fail in front of audiences — views counted, likes counted, comments visible. The fear of flopping keeps many from trying anything, and the shame of a flop can sting for weeks. The slang is light, but the fear underneath is heavy.

Answer the fear with the Bible’s failures. Peter flopped worse than any child ever will and was restored on a beach. Tell your child that failure is a normal part of a Christian life, that God upholds the one who falls, and that you love her flops as much as her wins. A child free to flop is free to grow.
roots_summary: Imitative flop (a heavy loose fall, 17th c.) → American theater slang (a failed show, late 19th-early 20th c.) → any public failure → Gen Alpha "flopped."
roots_lines: 17th c.: flop, a variant of flap — to fall heavily and loosely
Late 19th-early 20th c. American theater: a flop, a failed show
Gen Alpha: videos, jokes, tests that "flopped"
usage: "My science project totally flopped." "Then let’s figure out why and try again."
Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down (Psa 37:24).
Peter flopped, and Jesus said, Feed my sheep (Joh 21:17).

etymology: From goof, a silly or stupid person (American slang by about 1916, perhaps from dialect goff, a fool), with the adjective goofy following in the 1920s; Disney’s dog character Goofy (1932, first as Dippy Dawg) made it gentle. Gen Alpha uses "goofy" for silly or ridiculous people and things, often as a mild insult ("you’re so goofy"), and in the phrase "goofy ahh," where ahh is a minced spelling of a vulgar word — which parents should know.
biblical_def: Goofy means silly — in a fun way or a dumb way. "You’re goofy" can be a laugh between friends or a little put-down. Gen Alpha also says "goofy ahh," which parents should know is a disguised swear word. The Christian observation: silliness itself is a gift. "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22); there is "a time to laugh" (Ecc 3:4); and when God rescued His people, "then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing" (Psa 126:2). A family that laughs together is a family that has received a mercy. Christians can even be glad to look goofy to the world: Paul said, "We are fools for Christ’s sake" (1Co 4:10). But Scripture also marks the line where silliness turns sour: "filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient" (Eph 5:4) — the crude joke and the mocking word. "Goofy ahh" crosses that line by hiding a vulgar word in the phrase, and "you’re goofy" can cross it when it is meant to wound. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Being goofy is fun — God made laughing! We just don’t use goofy to make fun of people, and we skip the ‘ahh’ part, because that’s a not-nice word." Then he can be gloriously goofy with her.
webster_summary: American goof (c. 1916) → goofy (1920s; Disney’s Goofy, 1932) — silliness, a gift of the merry heart; turned sour in the put-down and the minced vulgarity "goofy ahh."
webster_full: GOOFY, a. (American slang, 1920s–present; Gen Alpha usage) Silly, foolish, ridiculous; often a mild tease or insult. "Why are you being so goofy?"
Goofy ahh — intensified form; ahh is a minced spelling of a vulgar word.
Goof — a silly person; goof around, goof off — to fool about.
Decode for parents: the word is fine; "goofy ahh" is not.
scriptures: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them.
We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
Eph 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
corruption_summary: Goofy silliness is a gift of the merry heart; it sours only as a put-down and in the minced vulgarity "goofy ahh," which smuggles a crude word into a child’s mouth.
corruption_paragraphs: Children’s slang often hides vulgarity in spelling — ahh, freaking, and others — and many children do not know what they are saying. "Goofy ahh" is one of the most common examples in Gen Alpha speech. It is a small thing, and also the kind of small thing that trains the tongue. The insult use of "goofy" is likewise small, but it can become a habit of mockery.

Keep the joy, drop the crude. Laugh often as a family; be silly together; let your children see you play the fool for love. Then gently correct the minced word and the mocking tone. The merry heart and the clean mouth belong together.
roots_summary: Possibly dialect goff (a fool) → American goof (c. 1916) → goofy (1920s) → Disney’s Goofy (1932) → Gen Alpha "goofy" and "goofy ahh."
roots_lines: Possibly English dialect goff — a fool (origin uncertain)
usage: "Dad’s being goofy again." (Dad is wearing the colander as a helmet.)
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine — be goofy (Pro 17:22).
Not foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient — skip the "ahh" (Eph 5:4).
